summary:
BKSpace is an educational space-mission game for Android, built with MIT App Inventor.

Players choose a target (the Moon, Mars or Venus) and design their own mission. They pick a real rocket (Falcon 9 or Falcon Heavy), a power source (solar panels or an RTG), an antenna and science instruments such as a camera, a spectrometer, a radar and an oxygen generator. Each choice uses real NASA and SpaceX data for mass, power and cost, so players have to balance weight, energy and budget.

After launch, players use arrow buttons to steer around meteoroids and space debris. They hold a shield to survive solar storms, while a progress bar shows how far they have travelled. After a soft landing, they drive a rover to complete timed science tasks while facing each planet’s hazards: dust storms on Mars and acid rain on Venus. Türkiye’s İMECE satellite also stands on the Moon’s surface.

The game also teaches sustainability. Debris from failed missions stays in the game and makes later flights harder. Players earn science points to build cleanup tools and switch to reusable rockets. A scoreboard tracks progress across all three worlds.
details:
What it does and how it works

BKSpace is an educational space-mission game for Android, built with MIT App Inventor. Players choose a target (the Moon, Mars or Venus) and design their own mission:

Mission design: they pick a rocket (Falcon 9 or Falcon Heavy), a power source (solar panels or an RTG), an antenna and science instruments (camera, spectrometer, radar, oxygen generator). The game checks whether the payload fits the rocket and whether there is enough power.

Flight: players steer with arrow buttons around meteoroids and space debris. They hold a shield to survive solar storms, and a progress bar shows the distance left.

Surface: after landing, they drive a rover and complete timed science tasks while facing each planet’s hazards: dust storms on Mars and acid rain on Venus. Türkiye’s İMECE satellite stands on the Moon’s surface.

Progress: a report scores each mission, and a scoreboard tracks progress across all three worlds.

Benefits

Players learn real engineering trade-offs between mass, power, cost and risk.

Players learn how conditions differ on the Moon, Mars and Venus.

The game runs on ordinary Android phones, so it is easy to share in classrooms.

Intended impact

Get young people, especially in Türkiye, interested in space science and engineering.

Raise awareness of space debris. In BKSpace, failed missions leave debris that stays and makes later flights harder. Players can earn science points to build cleanup tools (a robotic arm, a net and a drag sail) and switch to reusable rockets. This shows that sustainable choices matter in space too.

Tools and technologies

MIT App Inventor: block-based programming, with four screens (menu, game, scoreboard, developers).

Python: scripts that generate game graphics and build and check the App Inventor project.

Data and assets: NASA open data (Perseverance instruments, RTG power, planetary hazards) and a NASA rocket-test sound recording used for explosions.

Hardware: Windows PCs for development and Android phones for testing.

Creativity

Players don’t just fly. They design the mission first, and every choice changes how the game plays.

Pollution carries over between missions, so the game has lasting consequences that teach sustainability.

Each planet has its own hazards based on real conditions.

Including İMECE connects the game to Türkiye’s own space program.

Factors we considered

Accuracy: real data with simplified physics so the game stays fun.

Simplicity: we cut down on-screen text, because players don’t read long explanations.

Accessibility: large buttons, arrow-key controls and Turkish text.

Performance: keeping the game smooth on modest phones.

Licensing: we only used free or public-domain assets.
dataRefs: NASA Moon Fact Sheet: distance to the Moon, surface gravity and solar irradiance
NASA Mars Fact Sheet: distance to Mars, surface gravity and solar irradiance
NASA Venus Fact Sheet: distance to Venus, surface gravity, solar irradiance, surface temperature (464 °C) and pressure (92 bar)
Apollo 11: travel time to the Moon (4 days) and the laser reflector task
Apollo 12: the seismometer task on the Moon
Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicle: mass of the Moon rover (210 kg)
LCROSS: the water-ice search task on the Moon
Mars 2020 Perseverance: travel time to Mars (203 days), rover mass (1,025 kg) and the sample tube task
Perseverance science instruments: Mastcam-Z (camera), SuperCam (spectrometer), RIMFAX (radar), MOXIE (oxygen generator) and MEDA (weather station)
Perseverance rover components: low-gain antenna, high-gain antenna and UHF antenna
NASA Radioisotope Power Systems: MMRTG (45 kg, 110 W)
NASA RPS comparison report (NTRS): GPHS-RTG (56 kg, 285 W)
DART launch contract: Falcon 9, about $69 million (NASA release, April 11, 2019)
Psyche launch contract: Falcon Heavy, $117 million
Europa Clipper launch contract: Falcon Heavy (full power), $178 million
Mariner 2: travel time to Venus (109 days)
DAVINCI: the atmosphere measurement task on Venus
NASA SLS test-firing audio: the in-game explosion sound
NASA Eyes on the Solar System: the live James Webb position opened by the Webb button
projectRefs: İMECE launch announcement: İMECE, Türkiye’s first sub-metre-resolution Earth observation satellite built by TÜBİTAK UZAY, launched on a SpaceX Falcon 9 (April 15, 2023).
Falcon 9: the rocket used in the game for small payloads.
Falcon Heavy: the rocket used for Mars and Venus missions.
